title: Node.js streams: flow control, piping, and object mode
description: Readable, Writable, and Transform streams, `.pipe()` versus `stream.pipeline()`, what backpressure protects, and how object mode changes the rules. Each answer comes with code we ran in Node to check it.

questions.title: A Transform stream is a special kind of which base stream class?
questions.description: Name the class with both a readable side and a writable side that Transform builds on.

images.alt: A class map where each arrow means extends. Readable, a source you pull chunks from, and Writable, a sink you push chunks into, both lead to Duplex, one object with a readable side and a writable side. Duplex leads to Transform, a Duplex whose readable side is computed from its writable side. Four cards list the methods you implement: _read(size), _write(chunk, enc, cb), _transform(chunk, enc, cb), and _flush(cb), which lets a Transform push once more after the final chunk. A note says you call read, write, and pipe, while Node calls the underscore versions, and that _flush runs before 'end'.
images.caption: Transform sits one level below Duplex.

questions.explanation:
`Transform` extends `Duplex`. A `Duplex` has a readable side and a writable side that work independently. A TCP socket is the classic example: you read from it and write to it, and the two directions are unrelated. A `Transform` is a `Duplex` whose output is computed from its input. You write chunks in, and a transformed version comes out.

You can check the hierarchy yourself:

```js
const { Transform, Duplex } = require("node:stream");
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Transform.prototype) === Duplex.prototype); // true
```

So the chain is `Transform → Duplex → (Readable + Writable)`. `zlib.createGzip()` and `crypto.createHash()` are Transforms you have probably used already.

questions.title: What does `writable.write(chunk)` returning `false` tell you?
questions.description: A `write()` call returns `false`. What does that mean?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: `false` reports how full the queue is. The chunk still goes in.

options.text: The internal buffer has reached `highWaterMark`. Stop writing and wait for the `'drain'` event.
The chunk was rejected and discarded, so you must call `write()` again with the same chunk.
The stream has already been closed and will accept no more data.
The next `write()` will throw unless you pause first.

questions.explanation:
`false` is a flow-control signal, and the stream still accepts and buffers the chunk you just passed. It only means the buffer has reached `highWaterMark`, so a well-behaved producer should pause and resume on `'drain'`.

This shows the chunk isn't dropped:

```js
const { Writable } = require("node:stream");
const w = new Writable({ highWaterMark: 4, write(c, e, cb) { setTimeout(cb, 1000); } });
console.log(w.write("zzzz")); // false  (buffered length 4 >= hwm 4)
console.log(w.writableLength);  // 4      (the chunk is buffered, not lost)
```

You're allowed to ignore `false`, and Node will keep buffering. That defeats backpressure, though, and memory grows without limit.

questions.title: What does backpressure in Node streams protect?
questions.description: Backpressure is how a slow consumer tells a fast producer to wait. Which resource does it protect?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: The queue in the middle lives in process memory.

options.text: Memory. It stops a fast producer from growing the consumer's buffer without limit.
Ordering. It keeps chunks from arriving out of sequence.
CPU time. It caps how much work the event loop does per tick.
Bandwidth. It compresses data so fewer bytes cross the network.

questions.explanation:
When a producer outruns a consumer, the unread chunks have to wait somewhere, and that place is the stream's internal buffer in process memory. Backpressure is the feedback loop that slows the producer down: `write()` returns `false`, the producer pauses, and `'drain'` tells it to continue. The buffer stays near `highWaterMark` instead of growing until the process runs out of heap.

Streams already deliver chunks in order, and backpressure has nothing to do with CPU scheduling, bandwidth, or compression. Picture a fast tap over a slow drain. Backpressure turns the tap down before the sink overflows, and the sink is your memory.

questions.title: Which statements about `.pipe()` and `stream.pipeline()` are correct?
questions.description: Select every true statement. Both connect a readable to a writable, but they handle errors and cleanup differently.

options.text: Both `.pipe()` and `pipeline()` apply backpressure automatically.
`pipeline()` destroys every stream in the chain and reports the failure to its callback or promise.
`.pipe()` returns the destination stream, so calls can chain: `a.pipe(b).pipe(c)`.
If the destination errors, `.pipe()` automatically destroys the source stream for you.

questions.title: Which rules for writing custom streams are correct?
questions.description: Select every true statement about the underscore methods you implement.

images.alt: A class map where each arrow means extends. Readable, a source you pull chunks from, and Writable, a sink you push chunks into, both lead to Duplex, one object with a readable side and a writable side. Duplex leads to Transform, a Duplex whose readable side is computed from its writable side. Four cards list the methods you implement: _read(size), _write(chunk, enc, cb), _transform(chunk, enc, cb), and _flush(cb), which lets a Transform push once more after the final chunk. A note says you call read, write, and pipe, while Node calls the underscore versions, and that _flush runs before 'end'.
images.caption: Node calls all four underscore methods. You don't.

options.text: A custom `Readable` implements `_read(size)` and emits data with `this.push(chunk)`.
A custom `Writable` implements `_write(chunk, encoding, callback)`.
A custom `Transform` implements `_transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` and may add `_flush(callback)`.
A custom `Transform` requires you to implement `_read` and `_write` yourself, separately.

questions.title: In object mode, what is a stream's default `highWaterMark`?
questions.description: How many objects does a stream buffer by default when you set `objectMode: true` and leave `highWaterMark` unset?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: The blue note says the mark counts objects instead of bytes.

questions.explanation:
In object mode, `highWaterMark` counts objects, and the default is 16. In byte mode, the default is a byte count. It was 16 KiB for years and went up to 64 KiB in Node 22, so the byte number is easy to misremember. The object-mode default has stayed at 16.

```js
const { Writable } = require("node:stream");
const w = new Writable({ objectMode: true, write(o, e, cb) { cb(); } });
console.log(w.writableHighWaterMark); // 16
```

With the default, a producer can get about 16 objects ahead of a slow consumer before `write()` starts returning `false`.

questions.title: What does `objectMode: true` change about a stream?
questions.description: Pick the accurate description of object mode.

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: The mark changes units, and each chunk passes through whole.

options.text: `highWaterMark` counts objects instead of bytes, and each chunk passes through as a single value that is never merged or split.
Every chunk is automatically serialized to JSON before it is written.
The stream delivers data synchronously instead of asynchronously.
Backpressure is turned off, because objects have no measurable byte length.

questions.explanation:
By default, a stream carries `Buffer` or string data, `highWaterMark` counts bytes, and Node may merge or split neighboring chunks. With `objectMode: true`, the stream carries any JavaScript value (objects, arrays, numbers), one value per chunk, and `highWaterMark` counts objects. Nothing gets serialized to JSON. The stream passes the actual reference along.

Backpressure still works. It just counts objects:

```js
const { Writable } = require("node:stream");
const w = new Writable({ objectMode: true, highWaterMark: 2, write(o, e, cb) { setImmediate(cb); } });
console.log(w.write({ n: 1 })); // true  (1 buffered, < 2)
console.log(w.write({ n: 2 })); // false (2 buffered, hwm reached)
console.log(w.write({ n: 3 })); // false
```

This is why object-mode streams suit record-by-record pipelines, such as CSV rows or database results. They get the same flow control as byte streams.

questions.title: You write to a slow `Writable` in a tight loop and ignore every `false` return. What happens?
questions.description: You never wait for `'drain'` and never pause. You just keep calling `write()`.

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: Without the pause, the middle box keeps growing.

options.text: The internal buffer grows past `highWaterMark` and memory keeps climbing, because `highWaterMark` only decides when `write()` starts returning `false`.
`write()` throws a `RangeError` once the buffer exceeds `highWaterMark`.
Extra chunks are silently dropped to keep memory flat.
The event loop blocks until the consumer drains the buffer.

questions.explanation:
`highWaterMark` only decides when `write()` starts returning `false`. Node doesn't enforce it as a limit. It keeps buffering everything you write: nothing throws, nothing is dropped, and the event loop never blocks, because writes are non-blocking. The buffer just grows, and if the producer keeps winning, the process eventually runs out of memory.

```js
const { Writable } = require("node:stream");
const w = new Writable({ highWaterMark: 4, write(c, e, cb) { setTimeout(cb, 1000); } });
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) w.write("zzzz"); // all return false, all ignored
console.log(w.writableLength); // 20 — far past hwm of 4, no error
```

So respect `false` and wait for `'drain'`, and the buffer stays bounded. `.pipe()` and `pipeline()` do this for you.

questions.title: After `write()` returns `false`, which event tells you it's safe to write again?
questions.description: Your producer paused because of backpressure. Which event do you wait for?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: The right panel shows the event that lets writing resume.

options.text: `'drain'`
`'finish'`
`'ready'`
`'resume'`

questions.explanation:
`'drain'` fires when the buffer falls back below `highWaterMark`, so the writable can take more data. A typical backpressure-aware writer looks like this:

```js
function writeOne(stream, data, done) {
  if (!stream.write(data)) stream.once("drain", done); // paused; resume on drain
  else process.nextTick(done);                          // still room; continue now
}
```

`'finish'` and `'resume'` are real events that mean something else. `'finish'` fires after `end()`, once all data has been flushed. `'resume'` belongs to readable streams and fires when they switch into flowing mode. No standard `'ready'` event tells you to resume writing after backpressure.

questions.title: What is a Transform stream's `_flush(callback)` method for?
questions.description: When and why would you implement `_flush` on a custom Transform?

images.alt: A class map where each arrow means extends. Readable, a source you pull chunks from, and Writable, a sink you push chunks into, both lead to Duplex, one object with a readable side and a writable side. Duplex leads to Transform, a Duplex whose readable side is computed from its writable side. Four cards list the methods you implement: _read(size), _write(chunk, enc, cb), _transform(chunk, enc, cb), and _flush(cb), which lets a Transform push once more after the final chunk. A note says you call read, write, and pipe, while Node calls the underscore versions, and that _flush runs before 'end'.
images.caption: `_flush` is your last chance to push before `'end'`.

options.text: To emit any leftover output after the last input chunk and before `'end'`, like a compressor flushing its final bytes.
To discard the internal buffer immediately and free memory.
To force the operating system to flush the underlying file descriptor to disk.
To reset the stream so the same instance can be piped again.

questions.title: `fs.createReadStream(bigFile).pipe(res)` sends a huge file to a slow HTTP client. What keeps memory bounded?
questions.description: `res` is the writable HTTP response, and the client reads slowly. What does `pipe()` do behind the scenes?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable made by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response. Between them, the writable's internal queue is drawn as a fill bar with a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. In the first, the queue is at or above the mark: write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). In the second, the queue drains below the mark: the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring false only queues more chunks in memory until the process runs out of it, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: `pipe()` handles the pause and resume for you.

options.text: When `res.write()` returns `false`, `pipe()` pauses the readable and resumes it on `res`'s `'drain'`, so reads keep pace with the client.
It buffers the entire file in memory first, then sends it all at once.
It drops the bytes the client cannot keep up with and continues.
It blocks the event loop until the client has consumed each chunk.

questions.explanation:
`pipe()` links the flow control of the two streams. It watches what the destination's `write()` returns. On `false`, it calls `source.pause()`, which stops reading the file. When the destination emits `'drain'`, it calls `source.resume()`. The file is read only as fast as the socket can send it, so about one `highWaterMark` of data sits in memory at a time, whatever the file size. A 10 GB file streams in roughly constant memory.

The wrong answers describe the failures backpressure prevents. Buffering the whole file blows up memory, dropping bytes corrupts the data, and Node never blocks the event loop on I/O. `pipeline(fs.createReadStream(bigFile), res, cb)` works the same way and also cleans up and reports errors.
